title: Design the experiment
theme: Launching is easy. Knowing whether it worked is the hard part. Design a test you can trust.
practised: Choosing the right test unit and a fair split
Sizing a test and its duration
story_so_far: The First Order Promise pilot goes live tomorrow (Thursday) 8 am in Pune: 3 km cap, 12-item Fast Lane morning menu, +3 min morning ETA buffer, quality checklist with manual 'first order' stickers, manual ₹50 credits for late or wrong first orders; second-order coupons paused in the CRM. Earlier: failed first orders repeat at 6% vs 31% for good ones; Pune 7-day repeat of first-time customers is 7%; first-order on-time in Pune is 52%. Leadership review is this Friday.
world_today: Today is Wednesday of week 2. Meera wants the pilot run as a proper test so Friday's discussion, and the decision after it, rest on evidence.
canon_after_day: Test design agreed: Pune's 18 kitchens are paired by order volume and share of far orders, and one of each pair is randomly given the Promise (9 treatment, 9 control). New morning staff go only to treatment kitchens during the test. Primary metric: 7-day repeat of first-time customers (baseline 7%; aim 10%+). Guardrails: total Pune orders, margin per order, credit cost, complaints. Stop rule: pause if treatment complaints run 2 points above control for 2 days, or credits exceed ₹50,000 a day. About 3 days to enrol enough customers plus 7 days to observe, so the full read lands about 10–11 days after launch. Friday can only show first-day operational signals. Aditya's Pune 'Café Week' campaign is postponed by two weeks.

inbox.subject: Make it a real test
inbox.body:
Tomorrow we launch in Pune. I don't want to stand in front of Rohan and Anita with 'it feels better'. Design it as a proper test:

- what we believe will happen and how we'll measure it
- who gets the Promise and who doesn't, and how we decide that fairly
- how long until we can trust the answer
- what would make us stop early

Lakshmi can help with the numbers. Send me the design today, and tell me honestly what Friday can and can't show.

Meera

characters.opener: Ooh, experiment design, my favourite day 😊 Precise questions, up to 25 pulls.
characters.today: You know experiment design well. Help with numbers; don't design the test for the player.

hidden_facts.fact: To reliably detect 7-day repeat moving from 7% to 10%, you need about 1,350 first-time customers in each group.
hidden_facts.reveal_if: Asked how many customers are needed, or for sample size or power

hidden_facts.fact: Pune kitchens vary a lot: the 3 busiest handle 30% of Pune orders, and the share of far orders ranges from 10% to 60% by kitchen. A pure random split could put very different kitchens on each side; pairing similar kitchens first avoids that.
hidden_facts.reveal_if: Asked whether kitchens are similar, how to split them, or about fairness of the split

hidden_facts.fact: The cap and the menu apply to a whole kitchen, so the split must be by kitchen, not by customer.
hidden_facts.reveal_if: Asked whether to split by customer or by kitchen

hidden_facts.fact: 7-day repeat is a good early signal of 30-day repeat; in past data the two move together closely.
hidden_facts.reveal_if: Asked whether 7-day repeat is a good proxy or early indicator

hidden_facts.fact: In the two Bengaluru kitchens that trialled a 12-item morning menu last month, 7-day repeat was 21% against 12% in similar kitchens. It wasn't a controlled test, so treat it as supporting evidence only.
hidden_facts.reveal_if: Asked whether there's any earlier evidence for the menu or the Promise

tasks.title: Get the design inputs
tasks.description: From Lakshmi: what you need to size and split the test fairly. Check anything else that could differ between groups.

tasks.title: Experiment design to Meera
tasks.description: Hypothesis, unit, how you assign groups, primary metric, guardrails, sample size and duration, stop rules, and what each result would mean.

tasks.title: Handle the twist
tasks.description: Something will land in your messages during the day. Deal with it.

tasks.title: Set expectations for Friday
tasks.description: Tell Meera honestly what Friday can and can't show, and when the real answer arrives.

message.text: Perfect timing! I've got a Pune 'Café Week' Instagram campaign ready to go from tomorrow too 🎉 Double the launch energy! Cool?

ai_reply.direction: React in 2–3 lines. Probe one weakness (fairness of the split, staffing, duration or stop rules). Then ask: so what can I honestly show on Friday?

scoring.strong_player: Splits by kitchen because the changes are kitchen-level; pairs similar kitchens before randomising; spots that new staff in all 18 kitchens would muddy the result and restricts them to treatment kitchens (or explicitly accepts testing only the product changes); uses 7-day repeat as the primary metric with guardrails and stop rules; sizes the test (about 1,350 per group: about 3 days of enrolment plus 7 days of observation); keeps Aditya's coupon campaign out of Pune during the test; tells Meera Friday can show only first-day operational signals, and points to the Bengaluru menu trial as supporting evidence.

expected_answers.t1: Ask how many customers are needed to detect 7% → 10% 7-day repeat; whether to split by kitchen or customer; how different kitchens are; whether 7-day repeat predicts 30-day repeat; any earlier evidence. Check with Sana which kitchens get new staff.
expected_answers.t2: Hypothesis: fixing the first order (radius, Fast Lane menu, honest ETA, quality check, credit) lifts 7-day repeat of first-time customers from 7% to 10%+. Unit: kitchen. Arms: pair the 18 kitchens by volume and far-order share, randomly assign one of each pair (9 vs 9); new morning staff only in treatment kitchens during the test. Primary metric: 7-day repeat. Also track first-order on-time and complaints. Guardrails: total Pune orders, margin per order, credit cost. Size: about 1,350 per group at about 465 a day, so about 3 days of enrolment plus 7 days to observe: a full read about 10–11 days after launch. Stop rules: treatment complaints 2 points above control for 2 days, or credits over ₹50,000 a day. If 7-day repeat rises 3+ points with guardrails fine, roll out; if not, find out why before spending more.
expected_answers.t3: Not in Pune during the test: a Pune campaign with a ₹75 first-order coupon would pull coupon-driven customers into both groups and blur the result. Postpone two weeks, or run it in Bengaluru.
expected_answers.t4: Friday can show day-one operational signals: on-time rate, complaints, order volume, credit cost, treatment vs control. It can't show repeat yet; the trustworthy 7-day repeat read lands about 10–11 days after launch. Supporting evidence: the Bengaluru menu trial (21% vs 12% 7-day repeat, not controlled).

common_mistakes: Splitting by customer when the change is per kitchen
Random split with no matching across very different kitchens
Missing that new staff in every kitchen spoils the comparison
Letting the Pune campaign run during the test
scoring.senior_view: A senior PM would design around the unit of change (the kitchen), match before randomising, remove anything else that differs between groups, and say out loud how long it takes to know. They'd protect the test from well-meaning colleagues and give leadership an honest picture of what Friday can and can't show.
scoring.drill: Pick a change you'd like to test. Write: the hypothesis, the unit, how you'd split fairly, the one metric that decides, and one thing that could spoil the test.
